back: Two or more computers or devices connected so that they can communicate and share data, software and hardware.
The layout of a network: how its nodes are connected to one another.

front: PAN, LAN, MAN, WAN: what area does each cover?
back: PAN: a few metres around one person. LAN: one building or site. MAN: a town or city. WAN: a country or the world.

front: Star topology: main advantage and main disadvantage?
back: One failed cable or computer affects only that node; but if the central switch fails the whole network stops.

front: Bus topology: main advantage and main disadvantage?
back: Cheap, uses the least cable; but a break in the backbone stops the whole network and collisions rise with more nodes.

front: Ring topology: how does data travel?
back: In one direction round a closed loop, through each node in turn; no collisions, but one break can stop the network.

front: Why is a mesh network reliable?
back: Nodes have several links, so if one link fails data takes another route.
notes: A full mesh of n nodes needs n(n − 1) ÷ 2 cables, so it is expensive.

back: Client-server: central servers hold files and control security and backups. Peer-to-peer: equal computers share their own resources; cheap but no central control.

front: What does a terminator do in a bus network?
back: It absorbs the signal at the end of the backbone so it does not reflect back and corrupt data.
